stances.claim: Extradition has two distinct phases -- an executive evaluation by DFA/DOJ and a judicial hearing in the RTC -- and conflating their procedural protections is a doctrinal mistake.
stances.rhetorical_move: two-stage structural framework for understanding due-process entitlements

stances.claim: The extraditee is NOT entitled to due process at the preliminary evaluation stage because he is not yet at risk of being deprived of life, liberty, or property -- vindicating CJ's original dissent and the Court's reversal on MR.

Extradition is fundamentally a diplomatic process governed by the national interests of both states -- initiation depends on US national interest, and accession depends on Philippine national interest.
stances.rhetorical_move: elevation of the principle above procedural minutiae

stances.claim: Carranza's claim that BBM is subject to a US contempt judgment with a $356M penalty (separate from the $2B damages owed to human-rights victims) raises the question why the US has not initiated extradition -- a question pressed at Carranza and his militant Filipino-American allies, not assumed.
stances.rhetorical_move: Socratic challenge to advocates without endorsing the legal conclusion

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban uses the FBI's sex-trafficking and related criminal charges against Apollo Quiboloy as a doorway into a primer on extradition under the RP-US Treaty. Extradition has two phases: an executive evaluation by the DFA and DOJ of the requesting state's documentation, and a judicial extradition hearing at the Regional Trial Court. He revisits Secretary of Justice v. Lantion (Jan. 18, 2000), in which Justice Melo's ponencia initially held 9-6 that extraditee Mark Jimenez was entitled to due process even at the preliminary stage, over the dissent of CJ (then-Justice) Puno, Panganiban, and four others. On motion for reconsideration, the Court reversed itself 9-6 -- Justices Quisumbing, Purisima, and De Leon flipped -- and ruled that no due-process right attaches at the evaluation phase because no deprivation of life, liberty, or property is yet at stake. Panganiban grounds his deeper claim that extradition is 'essentially a diplomatic process' driven by national interest (the US pursued Mark Jimenez even though he was close to then-President Estrada). He closes by pressing former PCGG commissioner Ruben Carranza's claim that BBM and his mother remain under a 1995 US contempt judgment (extended to 2031, with a $356M penalty as of 2012 alongside the $2B human-rights damages) -- asking why, if the contempt is extraditable, the US has not initiated proceedings, and whether Carranza and his militant Filipino-American allies have actually pressed Washington to do so.
